chapter_mapping: The unit is chapter C2 Chemical patterns, with bonding statements drawn from C3 and calculation statements from C5. L1 = C2.1 (development of the atomic model). L2 = C2.2 (periodic table, Groups 1 and 7) plus C2.3 outcome 1 (Group 0) plus C2.5 (transition metals, separate science only). L3 = C2.3 (ionic bonding and the properties of ionic compounds) plus C3.1 (metallic bonding) plus C3.4 outcomes 8, 9 and 14 (covalent bonding and simple molecules), with an aluminium-corrosion aside that belongs to C4.5 (separate science only, so in scope for J258). L4 = C2.4 (formulae, balanced equations, state symbols) plus C5.3 (conservation of mass, relative formula mass, the mole, reacting masses). J258 has eight teaching chapters C1 to C8, C7 Ideas about Science and C8 Practical Skills.
assessment_structure: Four externally assessed components, 100% external. Breadth in chemistry = 01 Foundation and 03 Higher; Depth in chemistry = 02 Foundation and 04 Higher. Each component is 90 marks, 1 hour 45 minutes, and 50% of that tier. Both Breadth and Depth assess content from across all teaching chapters 1 to 8, so there is no paper-by-topic split. Depth carries at least two 6-mark extended-response questions; Breadth carries none. No lesson in this unit makes a paper claim, so nothing needed correcting on that count.
tier_rule: Only bold content statements are Higher Tier. Chapters C2 (all five topics), C3.1 and C3.4 contain no bold statements at all, so every statement this unit draws from them is examined at both tiers - which makes the two (HT) practice flags in L1 and L2 wrong. In C5.3 the bold statements are the mole and Avogadro narrative and outcomes 4, 5, 6, 7, 9 and 14, so L4's mole and reacting-mass material is genuinely Higher only and its wrappers needed widening rather than removing.
pags: No lesson names a PAG and no lesson uses AQA 'required practical' language. PAG1 (Reactivity trend, example activity: using displacement reactions to identify the Group 7 reactivity trend) is the only PAG that touches this unit; L2 states the displacement result but never describes an experimental method, which is spec C2.2 outcome 8 left untaught.
recomputation: Every numeric item recomputed and correct: Mr H2O = 18, Mr H2SO4 = 98, Mr CaCO3 = 100, Mr Fe2O3 = 160, Mr ZnO = 81, Mr CH4 = 16; 44 g CO2 = 1 mol; 0.5 mol NaOH = 20 g; 160 g Fe2O3 gives 112 g Fe; 80 g CH4 gives 180 g water; 18.1 g ZnO gives 14.5 g Zn. Every equation balances as printed: 2Na + 2H2O, C3H8 + 5O2, Mg + 2HCl, 2Fe2O3 + 3C, CH4 + 2O2, 2ZnO + C. All 20 knowledge-check answer keys index the correct option and every match order array is right.

findings.claim: A whole section, a key fact, an exam tip line, a knowledge check, two flashcards and a 3-mark practice question are built on Chadwick and the 1932 discovery of the neutron.
findings.truth: C2.1 outcome 1 names only Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr, and the teaching narrative adds only the ancient Greeks. Chadwick is never named in J258. The neutron itself is in scope (outcomes 3 and 7), so the material is not wrong, only unexamined. Left in place as enrichment; the practice question keeps its marks but loses its (HT) flag under F2.
findings.evidence: grep -i "chadwick" over both spec files returns no match; spec C2.1 narrative and outcomes 1-7

findings.claim: Question 6 is typed "3 marks - Explain (HT)".
findings.truth: Nothing in C2.1 is bold, so no statement in this lesson is Higher only. The flag tells a Foundation student to skip a question their paper can ask. (HT) removed.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/chemistry-b-21c-J258-bold.md C2.1: no bold content statements; chapter tiering note 'Statements shown in bold type will only be tested in the Higher Tier papers'

findings.claim: "Dates are commonly tested: Dalton 1803, Thomson 1897, Rutherford experiment 1909 (published 1911), Bohr 1913, Chadwick 1932."
findings.truth: No C2.1 outcome asks for a date. Outcome 1 asks how and why the model changed. The line sends revision time to recall that is never assessed. Replaced with a line about the order and the evidence.
findings.evidence: spec C2.1 outcomes 1-7

findings.claim: Rutherford is quoted inside quotation marks as saying the result was "almost as incredible as if you fired artillery shells at tissue paper and they came back and hit you".
findings.truth: His recorded words are "almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you". A direct quotation should be accurate. Corrected in place.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Geiger-Marsden experiments (Rutherford's 1936 Cambridge lecture)

findings.claim: Question 3, "Explain why reactivity increases going down Group 1", is typed "3 marks - Explain (HT)".
findings.truth: C2.2 outcome 5 and C2.3 outcome 2 carry this content and neither is bold, so both tiers are examined on it. (HT) removed.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/chemistry-b-21c-J258-bold.md C2.2 and C2.3: no bold content statements

findings.claim: "nickel (Ni) in catalytic converters" is given as a familiar transition-metal use.
findings.truth: A three-way catalytic converter uses platinum, palladium and rhodium. Nickel is barred in the EU because it reacts with carbon monoxide to form nickel tetracarbonyl. Nickel's standard GCSE catalytic use is hardening vegetable oils. Replaced.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Catalytic converter; spec C2.5 exemplars are copper, iron, chromium, silver, gold

findings.claim: "include units at every step - examiners deduct marks for missing units on multi-step calculations."
findings.truth: GCSE science marking awards marks, it does not subtract them; a missing unit means the unit mark is not awarded. The invented rule is replaced with the real consequence.
findings.evidence: settled fact about GCSE positive marking; spec 3a-3b make no provision for deductions

findings.claim: "The elements also become denser and have lower melting points going down the group" (Group 1).
findings.truth: Melting point does fall steadily (Li 181, Na 98, K 64, Rb 39, Cs 29 degC). Density rises overall but not step by step: potassium (0.86 g/cm3) is less dense than sodium (0.97). GCSE teaching accepts the general trend, and J258 asks only for the reactivity trend, so no edit.
findings.evidence: settled values; spec C2.2 outcome 5 asks only for reaction with moist air, water and chlorine

findings.claim: The 6-mark mark scheme says metals conduct "in all states".
findings.truth: Metals conduct when solid and when molten, which is what the point means; "all states" is loose but not mark-affecting, and the credit-worthy science (delocalised electrons always free to move) is correct. No edit.
findings.evidence: lesson practice_questions[5].marks

findings.claim: Outcomes in the mapped chapters that this unit never teaches.
findings.truth: C2.1: sizes and scale of atoms and the 10^-10 m order of magnitude (outcomes 4, 5, 6) and calculating protons, neutrons and electrons from atomic and mass number including isotopes (outcome 7); relative charges and masses of the three particles (outcome 3) appear only in one flashcard; the ancient Greek four-element stage of the narrative is absent. C2.2: Mendeleev reversing some elements against their masses (outcome 3), Group 7 states and colours at room temperature and pressure (outcome 6), and describing the Group 7 and Group 1 reactivity experiments (outcomes 8 and 9, PAG1). C2.3: limitations of dot-and-cross and 3-D representations (outcomes 11 and 12). C2.4: deducing Group 1 and Group 7 formulae from ion charges (outcome 2). C5.3: percentage yield and theoretical mass (outcomes 11 to 13, separate science only) and the 24 dm3 molar gas volume (outcome 14). Gaps, not errors; recorded for the build queue.
findings.evidence: spec C2.1-C2.5, C3.1, C3.4, C5.3 outcome lists

summary: Four lessons, 23 findings, 34 edits. The science is largely sound and every calculation recomputes; the damage is concentrated in tier flags and in generation artefacts. Both (HT) tags in the unit are wrong because no C2 or C3 statement is bold, while L4's genuinely Higher mole and reacting-mass content leaked outside its wrappers in three places. Two factual fixes: nickel is not a catalytic-converter metal, and Rutherford's quotation was paraphrased inside quotation marks. The rest are malformed knowledge-check stems, truncated match prompts, a spliced flashcard question, a stray 'StudyVault' token in four mark schemes and three invented or misleading exam claims.
